item.title: A native window
item.description:
go-widgets/window opens a real window and runs a widget tree in it: layout, draw, present, translate input intotoolkit.Event, repeat until the window closes.

w, err := window.Open(window.Config{Title: "Demo"})
if err != nil {
 return err
}
defer w.Close()
return w.Run(root) // root is any toolkit.Widget

Config also takes the initial size in logical points (zero asks for a readable default), the WM_CLASS instance and class, a Theme, and aRenderScale.

How Open chooses

Platform and environment Back-end How it reaches the screen
Linux, $GO_WIDGETS_GTK set GTK4 GTK owns the window; the framebuffer is a GtkPicture, and native controls are real GTK widgets above it. Needs the libgtk-4 runtime.
Linux, $WAYLAND_DISPLAY set Wayland xdg-shell over the compositor’s unix socket
Linux, otherwise $DISPLAY X11 the X11 core protocol over the unix socket, with MIT-SHM
macOS Cocoa NSWindow and NSView through go-macos/objc (purego)
Windows Win32 a top-level HWND through user32 and gdi32 syscalls, StretchDIBits
Android, $GW_ANDROID_SOCKET set Android host a framed protocol to the Java host, pixels in a shared memfd
Android, otherwise Wayland or X11 a shell under Termux still has a display server to dial
js/wasm, inside wasmdesk wasmbox a client of the wasmdesk compositor
js/wasm, an ordinary page browser tab a <canvas> of the page (Config.Canvas, default "screen") through webcanvas: no compositor, no SharedArrayBuffer, no cross-origin isolation
anything else — window.ErrUnsupported, so a cross-build still compiles

Every back-end is CGO_ENABLED=0. The X11 one is the core protocol written from scratch over the socket — no Xlib, no XCB — with both byte orders, the Xauthority cookie, keysym mapping, PutImage tiled under the server’s request size, and the MIT-SHM fast path, the shared segment passed overSCM_RIGHTS. Windows is reached through the process’s own DLLs withsyscall.NewLazyDLL and a syscall.NewCallback window procedure; macOS through the Objective-C runtime with purego.

The platform-independent part of each back-end — event mapping, coordinate maths, pixel packing, damage rectangles — lives in a codec covered at 100%,on every operating system. The thin platform glue is proven live: seeStatus.

Only what changed

A root that implements DamageRenderer (as toolkit/scene.HostRoot does)reports the rectangles it repainted, and every back-end presents only those:X11 through MIT-SHM ShmPutImage, Wayland through wl_shm damage, GTK4 through a partial texture update, Cocoa, Win32, Android, wasmbox and the browser tab. The first frame, a resize and an X11 Expose still present the whole surface.

On GTK4 this needs libgtk-4 4.16 or newer: the frame becomes aGdkMemoryTextureBuilder texture with set_update_texture andset_update_region, so GTK re-renders and re-uploads only the damaged region.An older runtime keeps the whole upload, chosen at run time. The framebuffer lives in GLib memory that the texture shares, so a present copies no byte on the CPU side (it was the whole frame, 128000 bytes for 200x160, every time). The GTK4 window follows resizes: the picture fills the window, the framebuffer is reallocated, one whole frame is presented at the new size, and damage resumes.

On the GPU

On macOS, Config{GPU: true} draws frames on the GPU.

  • How: the widgets are recorded throughgpupainter into ago-gfx/gpu2d list. Its Metal renderer draws the frame and presents it in a CAMetalLayer, without the frame returning to the CPU.
  • Exactness: the pixels are the CPU path’s, byte for byte.
  • Cost: a whole frame costs the processor 0.59 ms instead of 1.58 ms at 960 × 640, and 0.99 ms instead of 5.96 ms at 1920 × 1200 (Apple M4 Max).
  • Fallbacks: a window with a translucent material stays on the CPU path,and so does a machine where Metal will not start. Neither is an error.On Linux, see below; the other back-ends ignore the option.

On Linux (X11 and Wayland), Config{GPU: true} draws frames with Vulkan.

  • How: the same recording, drawn by go-gfx/gpu2d’s Vulkan renderer. Its pixels are copied into the window’s framebuffer, which is presented as ever:MIT-SHM (or PutImage) on X11, wl_shm on Wayland. The frame crosses the CPU once; nothing is shared with the display server by dma-buf yet.
  • Exactness: on software Vulkan (lavapipe) the pixels are the CPU path’s,byte for byte, proven live on both protocols: the window read back from the X server, and the wl_shm buffer the window committed, equal the CPU path’s.go-gfx/gpu2d measured its Vulkan renderer on a hardware GPU (AMD Radeon PRO W7700, RADV): Draw is 52 times faster than the CPU Rasterize on one core at 1080p; the window itself, with its copy into the framebuffer, has not been measured on hardware.
  • Fallback: where Vulkan is unavailable, or a frame is refused (too large for the device, device lost), the window draws on the CPU and keeps running.GPUError() on the back-end says why, and every later frame is a CPU frame.
  • Cost (software only): lavapipe is a CPU rasterizer, so the GPU path costs about ten times the CPU time of the CPU path: 25.8 ms instead of 2.48 ms per frame at 960 × 640, and 89.7 ms instead of 8.46 ms at 1920 × 1200 (X11,lavapipe on 16 threads in an arm64 container on an Apple M4 Max). Whether it pays on a real GPU is not measured yet.

HiDPI

The default is one framebuffer pixel per logical point: the UI is laid out and painted at a readable size, and the compositor up-samples it. On Windows the window declares per-monitor DPI awareness and the OS scales the logical frame to the physical client area. RenderScale asks for a framebuffer at the panel’s real resolution, which is correct only for a root that lays out in device pixels.

Screens, and showing and hiding

window.Screens() lists the attached displays, primary first, in logical points with the desktop’s panels excluded, and may be called before Open.A screen’s name is the panel’s own ("DELL U2720Q", from its EDID), falling back to the connector ("HDMI-1") when it publishes none — and also when two attached panels publish the same one, since a name that cannot tell them apart is not a name.

window.Show, Hide and Raise take an open window off the screen without closing it and bring it back — what a tray application needs.

Back-end Show Hide Raise
X11 MapWindow ICCCM withdraw, so it leaves the taskbar map, raise, _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW
Wayland commit again null buffer and commit ErrNotSupported: xdg-shell has no such request
macOS orderFront: orderOut: activate the app, makeKeyAndOrderFront:
Windows SW_SHOWNA SW_HIDE SW_RESTORE and SetForegroundWindow
GTK, Android, wasmbox, browser tab ErrNotSupported ErrNotSupported ErrNotSupported

Focus is the platform’s to grant: under focus-stealing prevention, Raise may only mark the window as wanting attention, and cannot tell.

Native controls on Windows

A toolkit.NativeControl becomes a real child window of the Win32 window, one per Key, reconciled every frame: a value is pushed into a control only when it differs from what the control last reported, so a person’s own edits are never fought. Besides the text, button, slider, progress and stepper kinds, five more are hosted:

Kind Window class Value
NativeList LISTBOX Number is the chosen row, -1 for none
NativeLink SysLink OnActivate fires on a click or Return
NativeDate SysDateTimePick32 Text is YYYY-MM-DD
NativeColor GoWidgetsColorWell Text is #RRGGBB; a click opens the system colour dialog
NativeSegmented SysTabControl32 Text is the selected segment’s title

The rows of a list and the segments are fixed when the control is created;change them by changing the Key. A link never opens anything itself: it only calls OnActivate, so which addresses are followed (http and https only) stays the decision of application.OpenURL. SysLink exists only in the visual-styles common controls, which a program without a manifest does not get; the window creates the link under a manifest of its own and, should that be unavailable,shows a flat push button that activates the same way.

Native tables, trees and tabs

Three more kinds carry structured data. Build them withNewNativeTable(columns, rows, selected), NewNativeTree(nodes, selectedPath) and NewNativeTabs(titles, selected); the NativeControl gained Columns,Rows, Tree and Revision for them, and Native.SetRows replaces the rows of a table afterwards.

Kind Cocoa GTK4 Win32 Selection
NativeTable NSTableView GtkColumnView SysListView32 (LVS_REPORT, LVS_OWNERDATA) Number / OnNumber is the row, -1 for none
NativeTree NSOutlineView GtkListView over a GtkTreeListModel SysTreeView32 Text / OnText is a path such as 2.0.1
NativeTabs NSTabView GtkNotebook SysTabControl32 Number / OnNumber is the tab, -1 for none

Sorting is not implemented: rows appear in the order given. A tab control is only the tab strip; the content under a tab is laid out by the toolkit as usual. The painted fallbacks (Table, TreeView with HideRoot, TabBar)draw the same data where no native control is hosted. The window back-ends that host these classes (hosted by go-widgets/window) arrive in the next window release; the Cocoa side needs the new GridView, OutlineView and TabView kinds of go-macos/appkit.

The data is bounded: at most MaxNativeRows (100000) rows, MaxNativeColumns (64) columns, MaxNativeTreeDepth (32) levels, MaxNativeTreeNodes (100000)nodes and MaxNativeTabs (64) tabs; a larger value is refused, not truncated.

Reconciling is change-only. The frame is keyed on Native.Revision(): while the revision is unchanged the rows are not walked at all, and the rows are pushed to the control only when it moves. On Cocoa a frame with 10,000 rows costs 160 us with an unchanged revision and 687 us when the rows change (including building the 10,000 rows); SetGrid itself takes 1.3 us because the data source is virtual. On Win32 an unchanged revision costs 0.26 ns and no allocation, against 43.8 us to walk 10,000 rows (measured on an M4 Max for Cocoa, one core).
